Analyst report · Q1 FY2027 · Confidence medium

The Star Entertainment Group

A genuine operational inflection: first positive group EBITDA (A$12m / ~$8m) since quarterly reporting began and the first YoY revenue growth at the two owned properties, delivered by EGM-led growth at Gold Coast and Sydney plus a 29% cut in unallocated corporate costs. But the equity remains hostage to a still-suspended Sydney licence, a Gold Coast suspension deferral expiring 31 Mar 2027, a A$260m (~$183m) AUSTRAC penalty payable over 19 months against A$239m (~$168m) of cash, and a going-concern uncertainty the company itself re-flagged. Shares +13% to A$0.13 (~$0.09) on the day.

A$284m (~$199m)Group revenue+2% YoY / +8% QoQ
A$12m (~$8m)Group EBITDA (pre-significant items)+A$25m YoY (vs −A$13m); margin 4.2%, +880bps
A$279m (~$196m)Owned-property revenue (Sydney + Gold Coast)+5% YoY / +9% QoQ — first YoY growth since Sep-24 qtr

Analyst report · Q1 FY27 · Confidence medium

The Star Entertainment Group

The Star's Q1 FY27 (Sep-26 quarter) is the first positive EBITDA print in more than two years — A$12m (~$8m) vs –A$13m pcp — driven entirely by the two owned properties (Sydney + Gold Coast EBITDA A$35m / ~$24.5m, +164% YoY) and a 29% cut in unallocated corporate costs, partly offset by the Brisbane operator-fee reset (–67%). The operating turnaround is real but small: a ~A$48m annualised group EBITDA run-rate sits below our ~A$70m estimate of annual cash interest (currently paid from a restricted reserve), statutory operating cash flow was still –A$15.5m, cash fell A$28m to A$239m, and the day after the AGM the Federal Court imposed a A$260m (~$182m) AUSTRAC penalty that triggers a WhiteHawk review event. The equity remains a levered option on licence restoration and Bally's continued support, not a cash-flow story yet.

A$284m (~$199m)Group revenue (Q1 FY27)+2% YoY / +8% QoQ (pcp restated A$280m)
A$12m (~$8m)Group EBITDA+A$25m YoY (vs –A$13m); +A$21m QoQ
A$35m (~$24.5m)Owned-property EBITDA (Sydney + Gold Coast)+164% YoY; margin 12.5% (+720bps)

Market report · Q3 2026 · Confidence medium

United States

Q3 2026 is the quarter the regulated US online market stopped being a growth story and became a share-and-margin story: iGaming growth slowed to a record-low 12% YoY (Citizens; ~13-14% on summed state monthlies) with no new states since Rhode Island, and sportsbook handle was flat-to-down outside the June–July World Cup window while CFTC-regulated prediction markets printed >$82bn of September volume paying zero state gaming tax. For an entrant the addressable regulated pool is large (~$6.5–6.8bn/month commercial GGR, ~$1.0bn/month iGaming) but closed-access, high-tax, top-two dominated and now contested by an untaxed federal channel.

Macau

Macau's 9M-2026 casino GGR of MOP187.12bn (~$23.19bn, +3.2% YoY) flatters a market that has rolled over: four straight monthly year-on-year declines through September (five through October), a Q3 of MOP60.22bn (~$7.46bn, -3.8%) driven by a 7.9% fall in mass/premium-mass baccarat, and GGR per visitor down ~5% even as arrivals rose 8.5%. The regime is stable but closed — six concessions locked to 31 Dec 2032, a 40% effective levy on GGR, zero licensed online — so for B2Tech the only realistic exposure is B2B supply into the one product line still growing, slots (+~19% YoY).

Market report · 2026 · Confidence medium

South Africa

South Africa is now a R84.5bn (~$5.1bn) GGR market whose growth is entirely online bookmaking: betting is 70% of GGR, ~86% of it online, and the land-based estate is shrinking. The rules are moving against the online channel — a proposed 20% national tax on online GGR (decision Feb 2027), new advertising norms, and an NGB site-blocking programme — while interactive casino remains illegal and licensing stays provincial. For B2Tech the prize is real but the licence-to-tax arbitrage that built the market is closing.

Market report · SEPTEMBER 2026 · Confidence medium

Tennessee

Tennessee's mobile-only sportsbook market took $591.9m of gross wagers in September 2026 (+4.7% YoY; taxable gross handle $588.6m, +4.9%) — the best month of 2026 but still short of the $598.6m booked in November 2024 — and yielded $10.88m of privilege tax under the only handle-based regime in the US (1.85% of gross handle). Growth has decelerated hard from the World Cup-inflated summer (+30–38% YoY in June/July) to mid-single digits, the licensed field has thinned to nine operators, and the regulatory story is now enforcement-led (a Sixth Circuit ruling that Tennessee's Sports Gaming Act reaches Kalshi's sports contracts, and a run of offshore cease-and-desists) rather than tax or licensing change. For an entrant, Tennessee is cheap to enter but structurally rewards scale and high-hold product; it penalises promo-heavy or low-margin models because free bets are taxed at face value.

Germany

Germany's Q3-26 gambling tax take rose 11% YoY to €622.1m (~$728m), but the shape — July +26%, August +12.5%, September implied ~−3% — says this is a World Cup timing effect on a 5.3%-of-stakes tax, not a step-change in underlying demand. The regulated market is large (€14.4bn GGR in 2025, flat) yet only ~24% online, with online growth (stakes +9–10% in H1-26) bought under a turnover-tax and €1-stake regime that compresses margins and leaks 23–80% of casino play offshore depending on whose study you believe. The GlüStV 2021 evaluation due 31 Dec 2026 and the 2027 licence-renewal cycle are the swing factors for anyone deciding to enter.

Massachusetts

Massachusetts is a ~$2.0bn (LTM taxable gaming revenue) mature, closed, high-margin market whose growth engine has downshifted: 9M 2026 sports handle rose only 2.0% to $5.99bn (online $5.93bn), with taxable sports revenue +6.0% to $611m carried entirely by hold expansion (10.2% vs 9.8%), while land-based casino GGR fell 2.4% to $880m on Encore weakness. The commercial picture is a DraftKings/FanDuel fortress (74.5% of handle, 78.5% of revenue) under a regulator that is now the most interventionist in the US on bettor limits and enforcement, with a live 51%-tax / prop-ban bill (S.302) and no iGaming path before 2027 — attractive for incumbents' margins, unattractive for a new entrant.

New York

September 2026 was a volume-strong, margin-weak month for New York mobile sports betting: a record-September $2.40bn handle (+5.0% YoY) produced only $159.4m GGR (-17.7%) on a 6.6% hold, the lowest September since launch, cutting the state's 51% tax take to $81.3m. The structural story is on the ground: Resorts World NYC's April conversion to a full commercial casino lifted statewide commercial-casino GGR 220% to $184.3m while draining VLT net win 37% to $124.8m. New York remains the largest, most transparent and most heavily taxed US betting market — a scale-only proposition for B2C, with the real white space in B2B supply to the three downstate casinos and in iGaming optionality that Albany has yet to unlock.
